blogs.title: When Threats Aren’t Enough: The Tenth Circuit’s High Bar for “Persecution” in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: This post would examine the opinion’s treatment of cumulative harm and why repeated death threats, an armed confrontation, an assault on an employee, and an apparent attempted abduction of a child still did not compel a finding of past persecution under substantial-evidence review. It would explore whether the Tenth Circuit’s case law has made nonphysical harms functionally insufficient in asylum cases, and what Jimenez suggests about the widening gap between doctrinal statements that physical injury is unnecessary and actual outcomes in threat-based cases.

blogs.title: Politics or Personal Retaliation? Jimenez v. Bondi and the Narrowing of Nexus in Mixed-Motive Asylum Claims
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s nexus analysis, especially its conclusion that any political motive was merely tangential to retaliation stemming from Jimenez’s involvement with Don Rafa’s property and alleged criminal enterprise. It would analyze how the panel sorted political threats from later criminally motivated threats, how the opinion applies the “one central reason” standard in a mixed-motive setting, and what this means for applicants whose persecutors blend political affiliation, local power, and organized crime.

blogs.title: Unable or Unwilling—and Unreported: Jimenez v. Bondi’s Demanding View of State Protection
blogs.description: This post would analyze the court’s government-protection holding, emphasizing its insistence on reporting persecution or showing with concrete evidence that reporting would have been futile or dangerous. It would discuss the panel’s reliance on the lack of formal complaints, its discounting of warnings from individual police officers, and its use of attempted searches of Don Rafa’s property as evidence of state willingness. The post would situate the case within a broader trend of requiring asylum applicants to produce stronger proof of systemic state failure rather than localized corruption or police complicity.

blogs.title: Internal Relocation as a Backstop: What Jimenez v. Bondi Reveals About Modern Asylum Adjudication
blogs.description: This post would explore the opinion’s brief but consequential discussion of safe internal relocation, including the court’s reliance on the family’s three-week stay in the Bogota countryside, the continued safety of relatives in Colombia, and the fact that the threats were framed as demands to leave the neighborhood rather than the country. It would argue that Jimenez illustrates how relocation analysis increasingly operates as a fallback rationale reinforcing denial, even where the claimed persecutor is described as politically connected and tied to organized criminal networks.
